---
title: "Blues for Guitar: From Roots to Shell Chords"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

This is how a guitarist plays chords in a band on a 12-bar blues without a single barre
chord: two or three well-chosen notes, moved by a fret at a time. You need to know how to
fret a note and how the strings are numbered (6 is the low E, 1 is the high E). For what
the chords are and how the form gets varied, see
[Changing the Changes in a 12-Bar Blues](blues-changes.qmd).

**How to use the page.** Every step has fretboard diagrams, a chord chart and a ▶ button
that starts the band. The diagrams show the neck standing upright: string 6 is on the left,
the nut is at the top, and the numbers down the side are frets. Click a chord's name above
a diagram to hear it. Under the diagrams the same notes are written on a staff. In every line of notation the note that is sounding lights up, whether the notation is playing by itself or the band is playing. While the band plays, its guitarist plays exactly the notes in the
diagrams, and the bar on the chart and the chord being played both light up. Tick **Leave
out the guitar** to take the part yourself. The strip at the bottom sets the key, the tempo
and whether the dots show chord tones or note names.

## 1. The roots

The **root** is the note a chord is named after: the root of G7 is G. Find the key note on
string 6. The root of the **IV** chord is at the same fret on string 5. The root of the
**V** chord is two frets higher on string 5. Three chords, three notes, and the hand stays
where it is.


In four keys (C, D♭, D and E♭) the key note is a long way up the lowest string, so the
diagrams start from the next string instead. Then the root of **V** is at the same fret on
the lowest string and the root of **IV** is two frets below that.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="roots" data-rhythm="pad"></div>

Play one long note per bar with the band and count the form: four bars of I, two of IV,
two of I, then V, IV, I, I. Knowing where the roots are is what lets you find every chord
shape that follows.

## 2. What the 3rd and 7th do

A seventh chord has four notes, counted up the scale from the root: the **root**, the
**3rd**, the **5th** and the **7th**. They do different jobs.

- The **root** names the chord. In a band the bass player plays it.
- The **5th** adds weight and not much else.
- The **3rd** says whether the chord is major or minor.
- The **7th** says what kind of seventh chord it is. Every chord in a basic blues has a
  major 3rd and a flat 7th (♭7), which makes it a *dominant* seventh chord.

So the 3rd and 7th carry the chord's character. They are called the **guide tones**. Play
only those two notes and a listener still hears the chord, especially with a bass player
underneath. The diagrams show all four notes of each chord, with the guide tones filled in.
Click a chord name to hear the four notes climb.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tones" data-rhythm="pad"></div>

### Where the flat 7 comes from

Why is the 7th of these chords called *flat*? The answer is in the major scale. Press ▶ to
hear each line of notation. The explanation follows the key chosen in the strip at the
bottom.

<div class="bl-scale"></div>

From the root: the 3rd is one string up and one fret back, the 5th is one string up and two
frets on, and the ♭7th is two strings up at the same fret as the root.

## 3. Guide tones on strings 5 and 4

Now play just the 3rd and 7th, as a two-note chord on strings 5 and 4. Look at the
**Superimposed** view to see what makes this worth learning: the three chords are the same
two-finger shape, one fret apart. From the I chord, move both fingers *down* one fret for
IV and *up* one fret for V.

That works because the 3rd of one chord is a half step from the 7th of the next. Going
from I7 to IV7, the 3rd drops a fret and becomes the ♭7th, and the ♭7th drops a fret and
becomes the 3rd. Switch the labels to chord tones and watch the two notes swap names.

**Up a tritone.** The 3rd and ♭7th of a dominant chord are six frets' worth of pitch apart,
an interval called a *tritone*, and a tritone turned upside down is still a tritone. So the
same two-finger shape six frets higher gives the same two notes of the same chord, with the
3rd and ♭7th changing places. Press **Up a tritone** to move all three chords there. That
gives every chord two homes on each pair of strings. In keys where the lower home would run
off the end of the neck (F and G♭ here), the diagrams start in the upper one, so the three
shapes always stay one fret apart.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="g54" data-view="super"></div>

The hollow dot is the root. Where one is shown it is in reach on string 6 and you can add
it; where none is shown, leave it to the bass player.

## 4. Guide tones on strings 4 and 3, and the root

The same pairs one string set higher sit under roots on both low strings, so every chord
can have its root added. These three-note chords are **shell voicings**: root, 3rd and 7th
with the 5th left out. A chord with its root on string 6 has the 7th on string 4 and the
3rd on string 3. A chord with its root on string 5 has the 3rd on string 4 and the 7th on
string 3. Mute string 5 with the side of your finger when the root is on string 6.

First the two notes alone:

<div class="bl-step" data-part="g43" data-view="super"></div>

Then with the root. This is the rhythm guitar sound of the swing era. **Up a tritone** here
moves each chord to its other shell: the root changes string and the 3rd and 7th change
places above it.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="shell"></div>

The band's guitarist plays a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3. Try that
rhythm, then try four even strokes to the bar (set the feel and tempo to taste).

## 5. The jazz blues

The last line of a jazz blues is a **two-five**: ii7, V7, then home to I, with VI7 in bar 8
to lead into it (the reasons are in section 3 of
[the changes lesson](blues-changes.qmd)). The ii chord is a **minor seventh** chord: its
3rd is one fret lower than a dominant chord's. In a shell with the root on string 6, that
puts the 7th and the minor 3rd at the same fret, under one finger.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="shell" data-chart="jazz" data-show="Gm7 C7 F7 D7"></div>

In bars 11 and 12 the chords change every two beats. Press **Superimposed** to see how
little the hand moves through ii7, V7 and I7.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="g43" data-chart="jazz" data-show="Gm7 C7 F7 D7" data-view="super"></div>

## 6. A tune: Blues in the Closet

Oscar Pettiford's riff blues. Its changes are the three-chord blues with a two-five in bars
9 and 10 and a V chord in bar 12. The melody is one two-bar riff played three times. Here
it is with the shells from step 4 underneath.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="shell" data-chart="closet" data-tune="closet" data-show="F7 Bb7 Gm7 C7"></div>

Comp under the tune with a short chord on beat 1 and another just before beat 3, and leave
the riff room. Then look at the guide tones alone. The riff's second note is the 3rd of the
home chord. In bars 5 and 6 it drops a fret to become the ♭7th of IV, which is exactly what
your guide-tone shape does at the same moment.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="g43" data-chart="closet" data-tune="closet" data-show="F7 Bb7 Gm7 C7" data-view="super"></div>
